title: A generalized lasso formulation of weighted and regularized (nearly-)isotonic regression on graphs
summary: In this paper we study a regularized version of nearly-isotonic regression with respect to a general partial order. In this estimator the sum of squares is weighted, with some of the weights allowed to be zero, and an additional quadratic penalty is imposed. The only assumption we make is that the quadratic part of the objective function is strictly convex, and we show that this assumption is mild. First, we show that for all sufficiently large values of the penalty parameter the estimator coincides with the regularized isotonic regression, in which the penalty is replaced by the isotonic constraint. Further, we prove that the resulting problem can be written as a generalized lasso problem with a design matrix of full column rank and with the penalty matrix unchanged. Next, we derive the dual problem, which is a quadratic program with box constraints, and write it in a sparse form that can be solved by standard quadratic programming solvers for sparse problems.

title: Nuisance structure and the detection boundary for population size: how profiling can change a rate, not only a constant
summary: A system contains an unknown number $N$ of units, each failing at an unknown common rate, each unit is removed once it fails. The failure-rate declines as units are removed, but after only a few failures the decline is too slight to distinguish from a constant rate, and the maximum-likelihood estimate of $N$ is infinite with substantial probability. This is a well-known feature of the model, but its probability has not been quantified. We show that about $N^{2/3}$ failures are needed before a finite population can be distinguished from an inexhaustible one, and that at this scale the profile log-likelihood ratio converges to that of a Gaussian shift experiment, in which an infinite estimate occurs with a calculable probability. The exponent is not a property of the model alone. Profiling annihilates the Taylor terms that the nuisance-parameters can reproduce, and detectability is governed by the first surviving term. For example, unknown drift in testing-effort reproduces the linear term, leaving a quadratic survivor and raising the requirement to $N^{4/5}$; in general the critical scale is $N^{2q/(2q+1)}$ for a survivor of order $q$. We obtain the limiting-law of the estimator, the null likelihood ratio distribution, and confidence sets that may be unbounded.

title: Recovering Hidden Wildlife--Vehicle Collisions from Existing Crash Data: A Cross-State Framework for Detection, Prevalence Estimation, and Under-Reporting Audits
summary:
Wildlife--vehicle collisions (WVCs) impose a large toll on U.S. highways, yet state crash databases often fail to record animal involvement, leaving agencies uncertain of the true missing count. This study evaluates whether existing crash records can identify individual WVCs and estimate overall unrecorded rates.
  We analyzed 4.9 million crash records from Colorado, Utah, Iowa, and Illinois (2007-2026). Each state's schema underwent a label-leakage screen to exclude explicit animal fields before harmonization into a shared vocabulary. Calibrated gradient-boosted classifiers were trained per state, interpreted using Shapley additive explanations, and evaluated for prevalence estimation via Adjusted Classify-and-Count and Maximum-Likelihood techniques across in-domain, cross-state, and synthetic reporting-gap scenarios.
  Detection performance depends heavily on record completeness rather than collision rarity. At ~4% prevalence, feature-rich Utah achieved an average precision of 0.88 versus 0.64 for feature-poor Colorado, and outperformed Iowa despite Iowa's 3x higher WVC rate. Within-state richness curves confirm feature depth drives accuracy. While classifiers ranked records accurately across states, probability calibration did not transfer directly. However, in-domain prevalence estimation recovered true collision rates within 0.001.
  This work shifts WVC analysis from spatial clustering to record-level detection and missing-data estimation using legacy datasets.
  Transportation agencies can retrospectively flag unrecorded WVCs, quantify total collision burden to support mitigation funding, and identify high-value reporting fields prior to revising crash-report manuals.

title: Multi-modal Laplace-based sampling
summary: We study the multi-modal Laplace approximation, given by a weighted Gaussian mixture centred at the local minima of the negative log-density, for sampling from probability measures that concentrate around finitely many modes as an inverse-temperature parameter $n$ grows. We derive explicit, non-asymptotic bounds on the Hellinger distance between the multi-modal Laplace approximation and the concentrating posterior. The bound decays like $n^{-1/2}$ with $n$ and the constants depend only polynomially on the dimension $d$. Moreover, we analyse the Laplace mixture as a proposal distribution for self-normalised importance sampling and independent Metropolis--Hastings (IMH) targeting concentration multimodal distributions. We derive asymptotic results, as $n\to\infty$, on the effective sample size in case of importance sampling as well as on the average acceptance probability, lag-one autocorrelation, and spectral gap in case of IMH. Numerical experiments illustrate and verify our theoretical findings.

title: Nonparametric GARCH: An Iterated Neural Estimator
summary: We study nonparametric estimation and forecasting for GARCH-type processes and propose an iterated neural estimator that alternates between estimating the recursion map and updating the unobserved conditional variances. Under mild conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for the time-averaged in-sample variance-path error and show that the estimator is minimax rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Under stationarity and mixing conditions, we establish the same rate for recursion-map estimation and derive finite-sample bounds for out-of-sample variance forecasts and expected excess Gaussian quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss. The convergence rates depend on the true lag orders and remain unchanged when the fitted orders are overspecified. Simulation studies illustrate the effectiveness of our estimators under nonlinear and time-varying volatility dynamics. Real-data applications suggest that our neural methods perform competitively and can incorporate option-price and high-frequency information.

title: BEAGLE in Action: Phylogenetic Likelihoods for Very Large State Spaces
summary: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

title: Mapping urban heat from citizen-collected data: a scalable Gaussian process approach to correcting for preferential sampling
summary: The urban heat island (UHI) effect amplifies heat stress in cities, increasing heat-related illness, mortality, sleep disruption, and energy demand. Because UHI intensity varies at neighborhood scales, intra-city temperature mapping is essential for assessing public health impacts, yet existing monitoring networks are sparse. Crowdsourced weather stations provide dense, hourly observations but suffer from noise and systematic biases, including preferential sampling driven by where residents install sensors. We introduce two scalable Gaussian process frameworks which adjust for preferential sampling and enable statewide, high-resolution temperature prediction. The first integrates sampling correction directly within a sparse variational Gaussian process (SVGPR+PS). The second uses a two-stage estimator involving a log-Gaussian Cox process (LGCP+GP) that estimates the sampling intensity field and incorporates it into temperature prediction. Both methods rely on inducing-point approximations and variational inference to scale beyond traditional Gaussian processes. Applied to approximately 10,000 citizen stations across North Carolina, the models generate hourly temperature fields within minutes. Validation against independent urban heat campaign data shows that the preferential sampling correction improves predictive performance, increasing average afternoon correlations across four cities from 0.26 to 0.43. This scalable framework enables neighborhood-level UHI assessment and supports studies of heat exposure disparities statewide.

title: A Tetration Distribution
summary: We introduce a one-parameter family of continuous distributions on the unit interval whose cumulative distribution functions are given by the odd-height power towers \(x\uparrow\uparrow n\) (\(n=1,3,5,\dots\)). The associated densities admit a simple recursive formula obtained by logarithmic differentiation. We prove that every such density is strictly positive on \((0,1)\) and integrates to one, thereby establishing that the construction yields a genuine probability distribution. Numerical investigation reveals a characteristic peak--dip--rise shape: a sharp mode lying just below \(e^{-e}\) for all examined heights, followed by a trough and a gradual recovery toward density value~1 at the right endpoint. We then identify the limiting distribution as the height tends to infinity through odd integers.

title: Terrain-Surface-Area Cover from LiDAR: Inverse-Probability-Weighted Estimation and a Global Cramér-von Mises Lack-of-Fit Test
comment: 32 pages, 6 tables, 3 figures. Synthetic validation; Lean 4 formal core. No real LiDAR or field data in this version
summary: Canopy cover is normally reported as a fraction of a horizontal map plane. When the domain of inference is the land surface, the appropriate target is the fraction of terrain surface area under canopy. We define this estimand on a C1 graph surface and show that it differs from vertical-projection cover by the planimetric covariance of cover with the area density, divided by the mean area density; the rumple index is a different quantity. A LiDAR pulse is recorded as a canopy return only when detection succeeds, so the naive return fraction estimates cover multiplied by the canopy detection probability. We study an inverse-probability-weighted estimator that uses that probability as the inclusion probability, and a weighted corner-averaged Cramér-von Mises lack-of-fit statistic for constant mean surface-area cover under independent canopy returns, calibrated by a parametric bootstrap. Synthetic validation on the flat plane and the Gaussian hill gives a naive bias near -0.40 and a weighted bias near 0.00; at 5000 pulses the test holds size at 0.02-0.06 across the simulated null cells and reaches power 0.79 under surface-uniform and 0.85 under plane-uniform sampling against broad slope-dependent cover, but only 0.12-0.13 against a compact hotspot. The definitions and their exact reductions are machine-checked in Lean 4. No field data yet.

title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
summary: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.

title: Scalable Bayesian inference for time-discretised Markov jump processes via exchangeable particle Gibbs
comment: 21 pages + 19 pages appendix. 6 figures and tables (+ 8 in appendix). Code and data available at: https://github.com/yanglanya980929/xPGTauLeap
summary: Inference in stochastic reaction-network models, such as the susceptible-exposed-infectious-recovered (SEIR) epidemic model, is crucial for understanding the dynamics of interacting systems in epidemiology, ecology, and systems biology. These models are typically represented as Markov jump processes (MJPs), with discrete, noisy observations and intractable likelihoods. Particle Markov chain Monte Carlo (PMCMC) offers a natural mechanism for inference on these hidden Markov models, but, even in moderate dimensional state spaces, particle degeneracy typically leads to poor mixing of the PMCMC algorithm. This paper focuses on improving the efficiency of particle Gibbs for inference on reaction networks by addressing the degeneracy problem. Building on recent work on the exchangeable particle Gibbs (xPG) sampler for diffusions, this paper develops a novel version of xPG tailored to discrete-state-space reaction networks, where randomness is driven by Poisson processes rather than Brownian motion. We focus on the $τ$-leap discretisation of the MJPs. The proposed method retains the exchangeability framework of xPG while adapting it to the structural and computational challenges specific to reaction networks. The new method is applied to several examples, including four coupled SEIR models, where it substantially improves mixing efficiency compared with standard particle Gibbs. In this example, xPG improves sample efficiency by more than an order of magnitude relative to standard particle Gibbs, making inference feasible in hours rather than weeks. As part of our tuning strategy, we provide a mechanism for tuning the number of particles that is applicable more generally, to any particle Gibbs algorithm.

title: Behavioral Prior Elicitation via LLM for Heterogeneous-Agent Bitcoin Flash-Crash Simulation
comment: Accepted on Conference on Optimization, Modeling, Simulation, and Analytics (COMOSA 2026)
summary: Bitcoin perpetual futures trade continuously with shallow liquidity and high price impact, making them prone to millisecond-scale flash crashes. Agent-based limit order book simulators are a natural tool for studying such events, but their behavioral parameters are usually hand-crafted or require full order book histories that are rarely available at scale. We propose a four-stage pipeline that constructs a reproducible 100 ms BTCUSDT flash-crash event panel from 66 detected events, elicits behavioral priors for four agent archetypes using an offline large language model conditioned on empirical microstructure anchors, instantiates a heterogeneous limit order book simulator with the validated priors, and applies causal discovery plus counterfactual analysis to the resulting synthetic panel. Across 500 simulation runs, LLM-elicited priors produce a crash rate of 0.176 versus 0.008 under uninformative uniform priors and generate heav- ier return tails. In the frozen counterfactual analysis, reducing leverage amplification by one within-sample standard deviation lowers the predicted crash rate from 0.176 to 0.136, whereas reducing directional pressure yields only a marginal change. These find- ings suggest that empirically anchored LLM elicitation can improve simulator fidelity and help identify plausible crash-amplification mechanisms in a controlled synthetic environment

title: Minimax signal detection in regression under differential privacy
summary: We establish minimax separation rates across sparsity levels for regression signal detection under $(ε, δ)$-central differential privacy, considering linear regression with an unknown error distribution and generalised linear models (GLMs) with an unknown intercept. Without sparsity restrictions, the separation rates for linear regression and GLMs with binary responses match the private Gaussian mean testing rate up to polylogarithmic factors. For GLMs with more than two possible response outcomes, additional information in the marginal response distribution permits faster detection of sufficiently small signals when the dimension exceeds the sample size $n$. Our upper bounds are based on a reduction to private mean testing, tests of dependence between the response and sparse covariate projections, and a response-only test that is adjusted for the unknown intercept. The resulting procedure adapts to unknown sparsity and matches our lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. We also construct polynomial-time tests that attain these rates when $ε\gtrsim n^{-1/2}$, and compare their numerical performance with existing private procedures.

title: Deterministic Uniformization for Estimation and Latent Trajectory Inference in Interval-Censored Multistate Triansition Models
summary: Interval-censored multistate data arise when subjects are observed at irregular visit times, leaving transition times and intermediate states unobserved. Likelihood-based inference for continuous-time Markov models often requires computationally intensive matrix exponential evaluations. We propose a deterministic uniformization expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm for parameter estimation and latent trajectory inference. By representing the continuous-time process through an embedded Markov chain indexed by latent Poisson event counts, the method enables deterministic E-step calculations without repeated matrix exponential evaluations. The M-step reduces to transition-specific Poisson regressions with exposure offsets, accommodating covariate-dependent transition intensities. We establish uniform truncation error bounds and show that the procedure is an asymptotically monotone generalized EM algorithm. Under standard regularity conditions, the estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Simulations demonstrate accurate estimation and computational advantages over direct likelihood optimization, particularly for complex transition structures. We also develop an exact dynamic programming method to calculate posterior probabilities of candidate latent pathways and identify the most probable pathway between observations. Posterior expected transition counts and state occupancy times provide additional subject-specific summaries, while expected-count ratios offer a computational shortcut for classification in simple mutually exclusive pathway structures. The framework supports both population-level inference and individualized characterization of disease progression.

title: Two-Layer Random ReLU Networks Can Separate Disjoint Classes
summary:
Set separation by continuous linear functionals is fundamental in functional analysis and convex optimization and underlies binary classification in machine learning. Support vector machines provide maximum-margin affine separators for linearly separable data, while kernel methods represent nonlinear decision rules through linear separation in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. We study when two classes, not necessarily convex or linearly separable in the input space, can be separated with positive margin by finite ReLU networks and by random ReLU features.
  At the deterministic level, we prove that positive-margin separation by a finite ReLU network is equivalent to the existence of finite closed convex covers whose opposite-label members have positive pairwise distances, and exactly two hidden layers suffice. For random separation, suppose each class is represented as a finite union of nonempty closed convex cells, possibly unbounded. If every opposite-label cell pair has positive distance and its closed difference cone is pointed, then two independent random ReLU layers yield a common positive-margin affine separator with high probability.
  The first layer separates the feature image of each negative cell from the feature image of the positive class by a hyperplane through the origin. It also controls all cross-class distances uniformly. The second layer combines cellwise scores through Chebyshev polynomials and realizes the resulting polynomial using Gaussian Hermite features, followed by a uniform finite-width approximation. With the remaining geometric, bias, and confidence parameters fixed, each sufficient width is quadratic in the largest Gaussian width of a spherical difference-cone section, hence at most linear in its span dimension. An example shows that this squared Gaussian-width dependence is sharp for both layers.

title: Tail reliability in probabilistic electricity price forecasts: comparing model combination and conformal prediction in the GB day-ahead market
summary: Probabilistic forecasts of day-ahead electricity prices are increasingly used to manage price risk, yet competing models are usually ranked on aggregate scores that average over the price regimes in which uncertainty matters most. This study evaluates probabilistic forecasts of hourly EPEX SPOT GB day-ahead prices over a full held-out calendar year, applying a common pre-auction information boundary and rolling-origin design to linear quantile regression, a quantile regression forest (QRF), a LEAR-QRA benchmark and an encoder-decoder quantile long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Two routes to more reliable intervals are then compared: conformal recalibration and Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA). Aggregate scores separate the LSTM and QRF only weakly, with a non-significant 4.4% difference in continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), but their conditional behaviour differs sharply. Above 200 GBP/MWh the LSTM covered 0.12 of outcomes and QRF 0.71, consistent with the forest retaining realised spikes in its leaf distributions while the network learned a smooth upper tail. Conformal recalibration corrected marginal coverage but did not improve the interval score or materially repair spike coverage. QRA combining the LSTM, QRF and LEAR-QRA forecasts reduced CRPS to 5.14 GBP/MWh and raised coverage above 200 GBP/MWh to 0.65 at unchanged interval width. Recalibration and combination therefore address different failures and are not substitutes.

title: A Bayesian-Geometric Reading of Classical Model-Based Optimal Design
summary: The classical model-based optimal design criteria (D-, T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality) are usually motivated via the Cramér--Rao bound as optimizing scalar functions of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). This paper offers a complementary reading in which each criterion appears asymptotically as $N \to \infty$ as the leading-order term of an expected dissimilarity between prior and posterior, with the FIM entering through the Bernstein--von Mises limit. The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of the posterior relative to the prior recovers D-optimality (classically known); a reverse KL of the prior relative to the posterior recovers T-optimality (here defined as maximization of the trace of the FIM, following one common convention) and its weighted-trace generalization; and a first-order approximation of the squared 2-Wasserstein distance recovers L-, C- and A-optimality. The five criteria emerge as instances of a common Bayesian-geometric template, indexed by three choices: the dissimilarity, the prior parametrization, and the approximation scheme used to evaluate it (e.g.\ Taylor expansions of the matrix square root). For the weighted criteria, the Gaussian prior covariance encodes the criterion's weight matrix, so any choice of weights corresponds to a specific prior in the family. The T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality derivations appear novel to the best of my knowledge. A sixth criterion, E-optimality, is recovered not as an independent expected-dissimilarity limit but as a min-max robustification of C-optimality against uncertainty in the modeler's prior direction. The framework is extended to distinguish between a designer's prior over unknown parameters at design time and a modeler's prior used for posterior inference, recovering the classical expected information gain objective as a special case.

title: Aggregate Calibration Can Mask Stress-State Undercoverage: Bounded-Memory Forecast Intervals under Recurrent Financial Stress
summary: Sequential forecast intervals are often evaluated by aggregate coverage even when calibration memory is bounded. This can be misleading when economically important states recur after long absences: a recent-only buffer may satisfy its overall coverage target while no longer containing errors from earlier episodes of the returning state. We study this problem in next-day financial range forecasting, holding the forecasting model, conformity score, adaptive update, and memory budget constant while varying the historical residual information available at each query. Recent-only first-in, first-out (FIFO) calibration is near nominal in aggregate but undercovers substantially during high-volatility states in both an exchange-traded fund development panel and a fixed stock panel. An unbounded state-history reference yields a lower observed stress-period interval score; Rare replay yields lower high-VIX interval scores than the matched Recent-n and Hybrid-n controls in both panels, and the state-structured versus recent-only contrast is largest near stress re-entry. Bounded calibration memory is therefore part of the forecasting information design, and aggregate calibration alone can conceal state-specific reliability failures.

title: How Risky Is Your Data-Driven Policy?
summary:
Data-driven algorithms are ubiquitous across industries, and there is an extensive literature on analyzing their \emph{average} performance. The risk profile of such algorithms, while critical, is much less understood. This paper quantifies the risk of data-driven policies and isolates its sources. We evaluate a policy through the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of its loss over the training sample, any policy randomization, and the future outcome, at a fixed unknown distribution. Regret against an oracle that knows the distribution decomposes into expected post-sample regret (PS), the average outcome-only CVaR gap of the selected action, and a sample-risk premium (SR), the additional tail risk omitted by averaging those evaluations. The analogous premium vanishes under expected loss.
  We characterize when the premium vanishes and how large it is relative to post-sample regret. For losses with a continuous density near the tail cutoff, we identify conditions under which both components decay at the same rate, yet the limiting ratio of the premium to post-sample regret can reach the thousands. When a probability mass at the cutoff moves with the action, the premium can decay more slowly and dominate post-sample regret. We establish conditions under which sample average approximation learns the oracle action at rate $n^{-1/2}$ in both settings, but its combined-risk regret is of order $n^{-1}$ in the first and $n^{-1/2}$ in the second. In finite-sample numerical examples of SAA in both settings, the premium accounts for approximately $74\%$--$97\%$ of regret.

title: Decentralized Sparse Quantile Regression
summary: Distributed statistical learning has recently attracted significant attention owing to its computational efficiency and scalability in large-scale systems. However, the non-smooth quantile loss poses substantial challenges to the development of efficient decentralized algorithms for quantile regression. Existing methods may either suffer from slow convergence or rely on smoothing-based approximations that require additional stringent assumptions, particularly in high-dimensional settings. To address these issues, we propose a decentralized framework that integrates gradient tracking with iterative hard thresholding for sparse quantile estimation. The proposed method avoids smoothing approximations and relaxes the initialization requirement. Theoretically, we show that the proposed algorithm achieves linear convergence under stated regularity conditions and that the resulting estimator attains the same order of statistical accuracy as its centralized counterpart. We further develop a decentralized information criterion for selecting the working sparsity level and establish support screening guarantees. Numerical experiments and a real-data study illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.

title: Sequential Bayesian analysis of time-varying transmission in stratified epidemic renewal models
summary: Understanding how transmission varies across age groups is important for epidemic surveillance and targeted intervention, but estimating age-specific transmission in near real time is challenging when infections are only partially observed, observations are delayed, and transmission varies across age groups. We develop a Bayesian age-stratified renewal model that jointly estimates latent infections, time-varying age-specific susceptibility, and age-specific contributions to transmission within an empirically specified contact structure. To enable sequential inference under these processes, we use a block particle filtering approach embedded within a sequential Monte Carlo squared framework, with fixed-lag smoothing to account for temporal dependence and delayed observations. From the inferred transmission process, we derive a next-generation matrix, effective reproduction number, and reproduction contributions. Applied to age-stratified COVID-19 surveillance data from Ireland during the Omicron dominant period, the framework reveals heterogeneity in susceptibility and transmission, with older adults exhibiting higher susceptibility, while younger and working-age groups make larger contributions to transmission because of their higher contact rates. These results demonstrate how statistical inference can provide age-specific transmission estimates to support targeted epidemic monitoring and intervention.

title: Inferential Issues in Model-based Small Area Estimation: Some History and Selective Recent Advances
summary: Model-based Small Area Estimation (SAE) has seen rapid growth over the past 25 years or so due to the rapidly increasing demand for reliable small area estimators of totals, means and more complex area parameters. Under a basic area-level model, we consider semi-parametric and robust estimation of small area means under model misspecifications. Under a basic unit level model, methods for estimating complex parameters, such as poverty indicators, will be presented, including robust estimation in the presence of outliers. A comparison of area-level and unit-level models when unit level data are available will also be presented. Estimation methods studied include empirical best linear unbiased prediction (EBLUP), empirical best (EB) and hierarchical Bayes (HB).

title: Nearly Linear-Time Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader for Weakly Observable Graph Bandits
summary: We study online learning with directed weakly observable feedback graphs and propose a Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) policy that achieves best-of-both-worlds guarantee with nearly linear expected time complexity. To preserve the simple structure of FTPL, we develop a novel graph-based loss estimator that combines forced exploration, conditional geometric resampling and adaptive learning rates with surrogate probabilities. Our policy achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(δ_*^{1/3} T^{2/3})$ regret for adversarial regimes as well as $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(δ_* \log T / Δ_{\min}^2)$ regret for stochastic regimes, where $δ_*$ and $Δ$, respectively, denote the fractional weak domination number and the suboptimality gap. summary: After variable selection, uncertainty quantification often treats the selected model as fixed, although it may change under repeated sampling. summary: A system contains an unknown number $N$ of units, each failing at an unknown common rate, each unit is removed once it fails. The failure-rate declines as units are removed, but after only a few failures the decline is too slight to distinguish from a constant rate, and the maximum-likelihood estimate of $N$ is infinite with substantial probability. title: Identifiability of Neologism Dynamics from Aggregate Corpus Counts
summary: Aggregate lexical frequencies reflect both what speakers do and how a corpus records it. We develop a stochastic framework for lexical adoption, abandonment and reactivation on a temporal multilayer network, together with a count observation model separating speaker prevalence, use intensity and detectability, and ask what such data identify. We give a necessary and sufficient condition for the never-active and dormant states to be merged exactly, collapsing the three-state chain to two, and show that the condition constrains the exposures a given network can deliver, not the response function as a whole. No count design can distinguish use intensity from detectability, an exact invariance distinct from the merely practical loss of information in sparse series. And we prove that in a low-prevalence community approximation the rates enter only through the net growth $β-μ$ and the coupling product $βκ$, so that a one-parameter family of triples has identical trajectories, the only separating information lying in a term quadratic in prevalence whose size depends on the emission scale. An exploratory analysis of 144 candidate forms in CREA and CORPES XXI press subcorpora illustrates the consequences: under the chosen emission scale and a symmetric contact graph, very different rate triples give nearly identical fitted trajectories, and in leave-one-country-out comparison with training-only proxies and seeds on a retrospectively selected cohort, a constant-rate count baseline beats the evaluated dynamic specifications on 84 to 94% of forms. These findings neither establish nor refute contact-driven diffusion. They delimit what this model and panel can support, and name the calibration, geographical contrast and repeated speaker observations that would make the question answerable.

title: Estimating "Realized" Skewness using Convolutional Neural Network
comment: This paper first proves that bias exist given a fixed-horizon of high-frequency data to estimate the low-frequency skewness by using the plug-in method. Then it provides an innovation machine learning method to approximate the optimal estimator by fixing a temporal aggregation architecture for neural network before learning
summary: We propose a new estimator of low-frequency skewness (monthly) that exploits high-frequency data (5 min) through a direct functional mapping consisting of layers of Convolutional Neural Networks followed by Multi Layer Perceptrons. Monte Carlo experiments involving stochastic volatility models, with and without jumps, show that the estimator reduces finite-sample bias relative to existing realized-skewness estimators and remains accurate under model misspecification. Empirically, our estimator exhibits temporal stability and delivers cross-sectional performance in actual skewness-sorted portfolios. We characterize the finite-sample bias of conventional plug-in skewness estimators and establish risk consistency properties of the proposed NN estimator under standard regularity conditions.

title: Covariate Adjustment for Time-Restricted Marginal Win Statistics in Randomized Trials: Assumption-Lean Inference and Guaranteed Efficiency Gain
summary: Hierarchical composite endpoints, analyzed through win statistics such as the net benefit (NB), win ratio (WR), and win odds (WO), are increasingly used in randomized trials to prioritize endpoints according to clinical importance. The Hoeffding--H'ajek projection of the two-sample win--loss U-statistics yields subject-level influence functions for the marginal win and loss probabilities. We apply treatment-specific linear covariate adjustment to these influence functions and propagate the adjustment to NB, log WR, and log WO. The resulting estimators are assumption-lean, remaining consistent and asymptotically valid without correct specification of the linear working model, and are asymptotically guaranteed efficiency gain over their unadjusted counterparts. Simulations with mixed-type HCEs demonstrate substantial efficiency and power gains with prognostic covariate adjustment. However, including additional non-prognostic covariates can impair finite-sample variance estimation and inflate Type I error, particularly in smaller trials. Bootstrap variance estimation improved inferential calibration in these settings. We illustrate the proposed method using a randomized acute kidney injury alert trial.

title: Conditional independence and graphical models for rankings
summary:
Ranking models define probability distributions over rankings and are fundamental in applications such as preference learning and decision-making. Without structural assumptions, these models are intractable due to their factorial complexity. Although independence assumptions are key to reducing complexity and enabling interpretability, standard notions of conditional independence must account for the mutual exclusivity constraints inherent to rankings.

This representation enables a well-defined notion of conditional independence for rankings and allows rankings to be modeled using Bayesian networks. As a result, standard methods for learning and probabilistic inference can be applied to rankings, with interpretable representations based on conditional independence. We further show that two prominent ranking models based on independence assumptions tailored to rankings arise as special cases, providing a unifying framework for independence in ranking models.

title: The Hidden Markov Ising Model with Exogenous Covariates
summary: The Ising model, a type of Markov Random Field, from statistical physics has a long history of modeling spatial and network data as well as particle interactions. In this work, we consider inserting the Ising model into the framework of a Hidden Markov Model, a type of Bayesian Network, to model temporal state changes in a sequence of Ising observations. While this is entirely a discrete probability model, a main challenge is the fitting of such a probabilistic graphical model due to the exponential intractability of normalizing constants within the Ising model. To circumvent this problem, we consider the usage of maximum pseudolikelihood estimators that have a long history in Markov Random Fields. Validity of the pseudolikelihood Baum-Welch algorithm, model identifiability under likelihood, and consistency for large networks is also proved. The proposed Hidden Markov Ising Model is further extended to incorporate exogenous variables resulting in a hybrid hidden Markov autologistic model with graphical dependencies integrated into the model. This model is applied to a five year sequence of weekly gun violence events across the 3109 counties of the continental United States to identify state changes in gun violence activity from 2021 to 2025.

title: Development of tools for all-cause mortality prediction in heart failure patients: a systematic review
comment: 26 pages and 5 figures, preprint and submitted for review
summary: Heart failure is a serious medical condition associated with risk of acute deterioration, recurrent hospitalizations and high mortality making accurate mortality prediction potentially valuable for patient care and healthcare planning. Numerous prognostic models have been developed using conventional statistics (CS), machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), but variation in study populations, heart failure definitions, prediction horizons and development practices may limit interpretation of applicability. We conducted a systematic review of mortality prediction models published between 2009 to the start of 2026 searching three databases (PubMed, IEEE and Scopus) for studies predicting all-cause mortality over a 1-60 months prediction horizon among patients with heart failure. Data extracted were cohort characteristics, heart failure definitions, model development, cohort size, validation practices, mortality, computational model design and reported performance. The risk of bias and applicability were assessed using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST). Of 1516 publications identified, 56 met the inclusion criteria. Publication numbers increased over the observation period, alongside increasing use of ML/DL models and decreasing use of CS approaches. Most development cohorts (64%) were classified as Unknown/Undefined heart failure, reflecting inconsistent reporting and terminology that did not correspond with established heart failure guidelines. External validation was reported in 23% of studies. Overall, research in modeling heart failure mortality has grown alongside increasing adoption of ML/DL approaches. title: Approximating Distributions on Vertex Degrees in Random Hypergraphs via Stein's Method
summary: Complex data are increasingly represented as hypergraphs. We establish bounds for approximating joint vertex-degree distributions by independent multivariate Poisson and correlated normal distributions in hypergraph models with independent hyperedges. We discuss the approximation of the distribution under different density regimes which are further supported by simulation studies.

title: Analytically Calibrated Upper L-Statistics for High-Dimensional Mean Change-Point Testing
summary: This paper develops upper L-statistic methods for testing and localizing a high-dimensional mean change. At each candidate split, the proposed statistics rank the squared studentized CUSUM values across coordinates and aggregate either a fixed number or a fixed proportion of the largest entries. This construction connects max-type and sum-type procedures and provides sensitivity to a wide range of sparsity regimes. We establish asymptotic null distributions under an independent-component representation allowing weak cross-sectional dependence. The limiting laws are Poisson tangent processes for fixed ranks and Gaussian-process or Gumbel laws for proportional ranks. To improve finite-sample performance, we develop analytic calibrations for marginal variance estimation, cross-sectional dependence, extreme clustering, and skewness, and establish their first-order validity. We combine calibrated p-values from a matched pair of fixed- and proportional-order statistics using the Cauchy combination rule to adapt to unknown sparsity. For localization, the estimated change point is selected from the component scan with the smallest p-value. Simulation studies demonstrate generally satisfactory size calibration, competitive detection power, and effective localization across different sparsity levels. An application to semiconductor manufacturing data further illustrates the practical utility of the proposed methods.

title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Includes appendices with proofs and numerical experiment details
summary:
Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order.
  In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-α}$, $α\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2α-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=Ω(nm\cdot m/n^{2α-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.

title: Post-stratified importance sampling
summary: Importance sampling is a building block of modern statistical computing, but the weighted estimate is prone to high or infinite variance. Moreover, its empirical standard error is often unreliable, leaving importance sampling without practical uncertainty quantification. Motivated by multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP) in survey sampling, we propose post-stratified importance sampling (PIS) for estimating target expectations from proposal draws. PIS reformulates arbitrarily high-dimensional weighting into two one-dimensional probabilistic modeling problems: regression for the conditional mean given the importance ratio and marginal density estimation for the importance ratio. Different modeling choices yield a family of PIS estimators, encompassing ordinary importance sampling as a special case. We develop a model-based implementation that combines one-dimensional Gaussian process regression for the conditional mean and score-informed heavy-tailed density estimation for the marginal law, using both the observed weights and the available density evaluations. We study the oracle gains of PIS and establish consistency under general and model-specific conditions. Simulations and applications to cross-validation demonstrate improvements in estimation accuracy and uncertainty quantification.

title: Statistical analysis of the remaining human life expectancy. Mathematical models of the type Gompertz-Makeham and others
summary: Many researchers believe that human lifetime on the interval (30,80) years is described by the Gompertz-Makeham distribution. In this work, the task is set to test this hypothesis. We consider a number of distributions: Gompertz-Makeham, Gompertz-Weibull, Logistic Kannisto-Makeham, Logistic Beard-Makeham and Logistic Beard-Weibull, some of which are partially known, for which comparative calculations on real mortality data are performed using the $χ^2$ criterion. The data were selected for three countries: England \& Wales, Norway and Sweden, cohorts born in 1900. As it turned out, on the interval (30,80) years the Gompertz-Makeham distribution is far from being the best among those listed above. In addition, for the same data, a similar problem was studied for the interval (80,120) years.

title: Conformal Prediction at Performative Equilibrium: The Price of Performativity
summary: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample coverage when calibration and test points are exchangeable, but exchangeability can fail when deployment changes the data distribution. We study conformal prediction in performative settings, where the deployed predictor affects the data distribution, and seek prediction sets valid at performative equilibrium: coverage must hold under $D(f^\star)$ for a performatively stable predictor $f^\star$. Under total-variation $L$-sensitivity of the distribution map, we prove a phase transition at $L=1$. If $L \ge 1$, no finite-sample procedure can uniformly guarantee both equilibrium-valid coverage and nontrivial prediction sets. If $L<1$, the minimax excess miscoverage over informative procedures is $\widetildeΩ(1/((1-L)\sqrt{n}))$, implying a sample-complexity inflation of order $1/(1-L)^2$ for fixed excess miscoverage. Our main technical tool is a transfer theorem: any procedure returning a predictor within $\varepsilon$ of equilibrium yields equilibrium-valid coverage up to an additive $L\varepsilon$ term after split-conformal calibration. We instantiate the theorem with two retraining algorithms: a model-free method for discretizable classes and a parametric tail-averaged method that matches the $n$- and $L$-dependence of this rate up to logarithmic factors. Experiments, including semi-synthetic credit scoring, demonstrate the predicted threshold behavior and scaling laws.

title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
summary: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: our review of leading journals finds that about 50% of articles state or imply LWD, versus 7% describing an imputation model. Assuming oracle regression with all required values observed consistently estimates the population average treatment effect, we ask when complete-case regression remains consistent. With constant effects, we offer two checks: whether covariates and the missing indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools valid within-covariate comparisons appropriately, potentially using inverse treatment-propensity weighting (IPW). For heterogeneous effects, assuming conditional effects carry over to the population, we reweight comparisons to the population covariate distribution. Simulations and empirical illustrations from American politics, comparative politics, and international relations demonstrate the framework's use and show why a missing-at-random (MAR) classification, although useful for assessing imputation, does not by itself establish whether complete-case regression consistently estimates the target population ATE. Thus, we recommend adding the missing indicator and its causes to causal models, then checking adjustment and weighting for LWD.

title: UniFlow: Unified Multi-Scale Flow Matching for Time Series Generation
summary: Real-world time series exhibit complex dynamics across multiple temporal resolutions, yet effectively incorporating multi-scale information into generative modeling remains challenging without increasing generative complexity. We propose UniFlow, a unified framework that integrates multi-scale representation learning with efficient non-autoregressive generation through a shared-semantic discrete interface. Specifically, a multi-scale tokenizer employs shared-index voting to consolidate complementary temporal information into a single public-ID sequence, while scale-specific codebooks preserve the information required for reconstruction. Building on this unified representation, we develop geometry-aware categorical flow matching, which initializes transport from learned low-rank anchors and generates public identities non-autoregressively. This design captures multi-scale temporal structure without requiring multiple generative token streams or sequential token decoding. Experiments across four benchmarks and both short- and long-term settings demonstrate improved generative fidelity, strong cross-scale consistency, and substantial inference speedups over representative autoregressive and diffusion-based baselines. summary: Heat-related mortality varies among individuals under similar environmental conditions, yet environmental exposure and genetic susceptibility are typically modelled separately. We propose a signal-processing cascade linking satellite-derived land-surface temperature to sequence-dependent heat-shock response and mortality risk. The framework combines distributed-lag filtering of thermal exposure, nonlinear HSF1 activation, cross-correlation with an HSF1 position-weight-matrix kernel, and Hill-model mapping of sequence-dependent binding changes to regulatory response. Variants in canonical arrays are significantly enriched for predicted binding disruption ($p=3\times10^{-4}$). Propagating these effects through the cascade yields a peak predicted mortality-risk multiplier of $1.68\times$ at $40$--$42\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The framework demonstrates how environmental and genomic signals can be integrated to model inter-individual variation in heat-related risk.

summary: We study nonparametric estimation and forecasting for GARCH-type processes and propose an iterated neural estimator that alternates between estimating the recursion map and updating the unobserved conditional variances. Under mild conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for the time-averaged in-sample variance-path error and show that the estimator is minimax rate-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Under stationarity and mixing conditions, we establish the same rate for recursion-map estimation and derive finite-sample bounds for out-of-sample variance forecasts and expected excess Gaussian quasi-likelihood (QLIKE) loss. Simulation studies illustrate the effectiveness of our estimators under nonlinear and time-varying volatility dynamics. Real-data applications suggest that our neural methods perform competitively and can incorporate option-price and high-frequency information.

For derivative estimation, we obtain projected derivatives of the Dirichlet density and their integrability conditions, extend the new bandwidth selectors, and carry out kernel mean shift clustering on the simplex. Simulations show that EMI is the most competitive selector for larger samples and Dirichlet-like targets, RSLS generally performs best for small samples and is more stable than LSCV for derivative estimation, and LCV remains competitive for non-Dirichlet targets in density estimation. Applications to wholesale customer expenditure and sectoral employment data illustrate density estimation and clustering, respectively.

title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding
summary: We study a fundamental problem in machine learning: partial recovery of a planted signal $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ from a spiked tensor $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}} = λ\, \boldsymbol{v}^{\otimes p} + \boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ has symmetric Gaussian entries of variance $\asymp n^{-1}$. We show that the square unfolding algorithm is subject to a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $λ\asymp n^{(p-2) / 4}$, validating an open conjecture from Montanari and Richard (2014). The main message is that unfolded symmetric tensors spectrally behave like standard Wigner matrices, up to simple transformations accounting for high-order symmetries. We consider extensions to multiple orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding via disproportionate random matrix theory, leading to an interesting conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff regarding the choice of unfolding: square versus long.

A decay prediction model achieves C-index $= 0.93$ on held-out factor pairs, providing early warning of signal erosion---the key predictor is initial signal strength: stronger signals decay faster (``regression to the mean''). summary: This paper investigates the determinants of head coach turnover in the Italian Serie A over the period 2010-2019 by explicitly accounting for multiple exit mechanisms within a competing risks framework. Four mutually exclusive exit types are considered: end of contract, mutual consent, resignation, and sacking. To identify robust predictors of turnover, we combine classical cause-specific Cox models with a variable selection procedure based on forward selection, LASSO regression, and Random Survival Forests. The results show that performance-related variables are the primary drivers of coach turnover, while personal characteristics play a limited role once performance is controlled for. Short-term performance indicators, such as points per match until turnover, strongly influence the risk of dismissal. Conversely, cumulative poor performance substantially increases dismissal risk: a higher proportion of losses over a coach's tenure raises the hazard of sacking by more than four times. Season timing also plays a crucial role, as sackings and mutual-consent terminations are significantly more likely to occur during the season, whereas contract expirations concentrate at the end of the season. Overall, the findings highlight that clubs differentiate between short-term performance shocks and longer-term performance trajectories when deciding how and when to replace a head coach. By distinguishing among exit mechanisms and adopting a conservative variable selection strategy, the study provides a robust and nuanced assessment of managerial turnover dynamics in the most important Italian professional football league.

title: Separating Weight and Likelihood Tail Effects in Bayesian Neural Groundwater Inversion
summary: Groundwater inversion is commonly built on Gaussian assumptions for both network weights and output errors. The assumptions are convenient, but it is unclear which one should be relaxed when hydraulic conductivity is heavy tailed. Here, Gaussian and q-Gaussian distributions were assigned independently to variational weights and the conditional output likelihood in a $2\times2$ Bayesian neural design. Hydraulic conductivity, porosity, and dispersion were inferred jointly from sparse head and transport observations. Four q regimes ($q=1.0$, 1.2, 1.5, and 1.8) were evaluated with five independently generated data sets and matched training seeds, giving 130 held-out cases per regime and 500 posterior draws per case. At $q=1.5$, q-Gaussian weights with a Gaussian likelihood reduced log-conductivity CRPS by 2.85\% (95\% paired CI 0.82--4.88) and calibration error by 3.72 percentage points. Conductivity RMSE was unchanged, while 95\% interval width increased by 9.86\%. At $q=1.8$, assigning q-Gaussian tails to both components produced no stable accuracy gain and increased interval width by 138.46\%. The Gaussian-generated porosity and dispersion controls showed negligible accuracy changes. Moderate weight-side tails can thus improve distributional prediction, whereas an overly heavy output likelihood trades sharpness for coverage. Separating these two roles provides a clearer basis for uncertainty modeling in groundwater inversion.

title: Inferential Issues in Model-based Small Area Estimation: Some History and Selective Recent Advances
summary: Model-based Small Area Estimation (SAE) has seen rapid growth over the past 25 years or so due to the rapidly increasing demand for reliable small area estimators of totals, means and more complex area parameters. Direct area-specific estimators are either unreliable (due to small area-specific sample sizes) or not feasible (due to zero area-specific sample sizes). It is therefore necessary to borrow strength from related areas through implicit or explicit models linking related areas. We focus on explicit area-level and unit-level models. After a brief historical sketch of the evolution of SAE, we focus on selective recent developments (mostly after 2015). Developments before 2015 are mostly covered in the comprehensive Wiley book by Rao and Molina (2015). Under a basic area-level model, we consider semi-parametric and robust estimation of small area means under model misspecifications. Under a basic unit level model, methods for estimating complex parameters, such as poverty indicators, will be presented, including robust estimation in the presence of outliers. A comparison of area-level and unit-level models when unit level data are available will also be presented. Estimation methods studied include empirical best linear unbiased prediction (EBLUP), empirical best (EB) and hierarchical Bayes (HB).

title: Decentralized Sparse Quantile Regression
summary: Distributed statistical learning has recently attracted significant attention owing to its computational efficiency and scalability in large-scale systems. However, the non-smooth quantile loss poses substantial challenges to the development of efficient decentralized algorithms for quantile regression. Existing methods may either suffer from slow convergence or rely on smoothing-based approximations that require additional stringent assumptions, particularly in high-dimensional settings. To address these issues, we propose a decentralized framework that integrates gradient tracking with iterative hard thresholding for sparse quantile estimation. The proposed method avoids smoothing approximations and relaxes the initialization requirement. Theoretically, we show that the proposed algorithm achieves linear convergence under stated regularity conditions and that the resulting estimator attains the same order of statistical accuracy as its centralized counterpart. We further develop a decentralized information criterion for selecting the working sparsity level and establish support screening guarantees. Numerical experiments and a real-data study illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed method.

title: A reliability data aggregation method for fusion-oriented research facilities
summary: This paper aims to develop a statistical method for integrating multiple incomplete data sources to improve the estimation of the failure-rate probability distribution of fusion-specific devices. The data aggregation approach proposed in this work is to support the Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Inspectability (RAMI) studies for fusion-oriented research facilities. This work focuses on developing a procedure for handling missing or incomplete data from multiple sources, as well as formulating a statistical framework for combining data from different sources that refer to the same equipment type and failure mode. Specifically, a Bayesian result is adopted under the assumption of a constant failure rate over time. This framework motivates the use of the Gamma distributions to model the failure-rate parameter of each device. Subsequently, two alternative procedures are introduced to approximate, using a single Gamma distribution, the weighted mixture formed by combining Gamma distributions corresponding to the same equipment type across multiple data sources. The proposed method is validated through an extensive simulation study and further illustrated by application to the accelerator systems of the IFMIF-DONES facility. Finally, the proposed algorithm has been implemented in the open-source software R to facilitate its use in the nuclear fusion community.

title: A Bayesian-Geometric Reading of Classical Model-Based Optimal Design
summary: The classical model-based optimal design criteria (D-, T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality) are usually motivated via the Cramér--Rao bound as optimizing scalar functions of the Fisher information matrix (FIM). This paper offers a complementary reading in which each criterion appears asymptotically as $N \to \infty$ as the leading-order term of an expected dissimilarity between prior and posterior, with the FIM entering through the Bernstein--von Mises limit. The Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence of the posterior relative to the prior recovers D-optimality (classically known); a reverse KL of the prior relative to the posterior recovers T-optimality (here defined as maximization of the trace of the FIM, following one common convention) and its weighted-trace generalization; and a first-order approximation of the squared 2-Wasserstein distance recovers L-, C- and A-optimality. The five criteria emerge as instances of a common Bayesian-geometric template, indexed by three choices: the dissimilarity, the prior parametrization, and the approximation scheme used to evaluate it (e.g.\ Taylor expansions of the matrix square root). For the weighted criteria, the Gaussian prior covariance encodes the criterion's weight matrix, so any choice of weights corresponds to a specific prior in the family. The T-, L-, C-, and A-optimality derivations appear novel to the best of my knowledge. A sixth criterion, E-optimality, is recovered not as an independent expected-dissimilarity limit but as a min-max robustification of C-optimality against uncertainty in the modeler's prior direction. The framework is extended to distinguish between a designer's prior over unknown parameters at design time and a modeler's prior used for posterior inference, recovering the classical expected information gain objective as a special case.

title: Integrating Machine Learning and Uncertainty Quantification for Real-Time Decision-Making in Digital Twins: A System-Centric Review and Perspective
summary: Digital Twins are evolving from passive virtual representations into closed-loop systems that continuously synchronize with physical assets and drive real-time decisions. Yet predictive modeling, machine learning (ML), uncertainty quantification (UQ), and decision-making have been studied as separate capabilities, leaving limited understanding of their integration and maintenance during online operation. This narrative review, scoped by the functional requirements of real-time decision-making rather than by Digital Twin terminology alone, examines how such decisions are generated and sustained in engineering Digital Twins. We first examine foundational decision-making architectures and representative engineering applications, followed by methods that address their limitations across the decision loop. We identify optimization-based, policy-based, and knowledge-based approaches as the major pathways from virtual representation to action. Across them, ML plays three roles in decision-making: enabling efficient surrogate modeling, transforming heterogeneous physical feedback into decision-relevant information, and accelerating or directly generating decisions. UQ supports uncertainty-aware decisions and model adaptation, while continual validation, drift detection, and adaptation help maintain reliable operation as the physical system evolves. Together, these findings underscore the need for a shift from a model-centric to a system-centric perspective on Digital Twins, where its performance depends on the interactions with sensing, state estimation, computation, decision-making, and adaptation rather than on their standalone performance. Therefore, future research should shift from isolated algorithm development toward system-level co-design, scalable decision-making, and approaches to design, and data-efficient continual adaptation and validation for AI-enabled autonomous systems.
